tips.title: Four symbols, and the shape is the meaning
tips.body: A **rounded box** starts or stops. A **rectangle** is a process. A **parallelogram** is input or output. A **diamond** is a decision. The shape carries the meaning, so drawing the wrong one says the wrong thing however good the label is.

tips.title: Every decision needs two labelled exits
tips.body: A diamond with one arrow out is not a decision. Both paths must leave it and both must be **labelled** — usually Yes and No. An unlabelled exit is the most common way to lose a mark on a flowchart question.

tips.title: A loop is an arrow going back up
tips.body: Iteration in a flowchart is a **decision with an arrow returning to an earlier box**. If you cannot find an arrow pointing upwards, the algorithm has no loop in it, whatever the labels say.

tips.title: You may answer in any sensible format
tips.body: Pseudo-code you are **given** will be AQA's own version, so you must be able to read it. But when pseudo-code is an accepted response, the specification says you **do not have to use AQA pseudo-code** — any clear, consistent notation is accepted.

tips.title: Read the question for the form wanted
tips.body: The specification says exam questions **indicate the form of response expected** — pseudo-code, program code, or a flowchart. Answering in the wrong form is not a partial answer; it is the wrong answer, and it is entirely avoidable.

steps.title: Three ways to write an algorithm
steps.body:
**An algorithm is a sequence of steps that can be followed to complete a task.** The specification is careful to add that **a computer program is an implementation of an algorithm, and an algorithm is not a computer program** — the algorithm is the plan, and the program is one way of carrying it out.

The specification names **three** ways of representing one:

- **pseudo-code** — code-like text that no computer runs
- **program code** — a real language, such as Python, C# or VB.NET
- **a flowchart** — boxes and arrows

**Each suits a different job.** A flowchart shows the *shape* of an algorithm at a glance, especially its branches and loops. Pseudo-code is quicker to write and closer to code. Program code actually runs but ties you to one language.

**Two things about the exam are worth knowing exactly.**

> **Any exam question where students are given pseudo-code will use the AQA standard version.**

So you must be able to **read** AQA pseudo-code. But:

> **Where pseudo-code is an accepted method of response, students may present their answers in any suitable format and do not need to use the AQA pseudo-code.**

So you do not have to **write** it. And the specification also says questions **indicate the form of response expected**, so read the question and give the form it asks for.

options: An algorithm is the sequence of steps; a program is one implementation of it
An algorithm runs on a computer and a program does not
An algorithm is written in pseudo-code and a program in a flowchart
There is no difference between the two terms
check.solution: An algorithm is **a sequence of steps that can be followed to complete a task**. A program is an **implementation** of one, in a particular language. The same algorithm can be implemented many times over.

steps.title: The four flowchart symbols
steps.body:
**A flowchart carries its meaning in the shapes**, so each one has a job:

| Symbol | Shape | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| terminal | rounded box | START and STOP |
| process | rectangle | a calculation or an assignment |
| input/output | parallelogram | INPUT and OUTPUT |
| decision | diamond | a question with two answers |

**Arrows join them, and they show the order of the steps.**

**A decision is the one with a rule attached: it must have exactly two exits, and both must be labelled** — normally **Yes** and **No**. A diamond with a single arrow leaving it is not a decision at all, and a pair of unlabelled exits leaves the reader guessing which is which.

**Every flowchart starts and stops with a terminal.** An algorithm that never stops is a fault, not a style.

**Watch the difference between a process and an input/output.** Working something out is a **process** — a rectangle. Getting a value from the user, or showing one to them, is **input/output** — a parallelogram. `n ← n * 2` is a process; `OUTPUT n` is not.

steps.title: The same algorithm, both ways
steps.body:
**A flowchart and pseudo-code can say exactly the same thing.** Being able to move between them is what the specification means by representing algorithms.

The algorithm below starts at 1, doubles until it reaches 50 or more, and outputs the result. Notice how each part of the flowchart maps onto a line of the pseudo-code.

visuals.alt: A full flowchart: START, set n to 1, a decision asking if n is less than 50; the Yes path doubles n and returns to the decision, and the No path leads past it to OUTPUT n and STOP

visuals.problem: Write the flowchart above as AQA pseudo-code.

steps.text: The terminal boxes are not written: pseudo-code simply begins and ends
steps.note: START and STOP exist to make a flowchart readable, not as instructions

steps.text:
The first process box becomes an assignment:

```
n ← 1
```
steps.note: AQA uses a left arrow for assignment, not an equals sign

steps.text:
The decision with a loop back becomes a WHILE:

```
WHILE n < 50
   n ← n * 2
ENDWHILE
```
steps.note: a decision whose Yes path returns to an earlier box is indefinite iteration

steps.text:
The parallelogram becomes an output:

```
OUTPUT n
```
steps.note: the parallelogram is the giveaway that this is output, not a calculation

steps.text: Putting it together gives the whole algorithm, and it outputs **64**
steps.note: the loop stops at the first value that is 50 or more

check.prompt: A flowchart has a decision whose Yes path leads back to an earlier box. Which pseudo-code structure does that represent?
check.skill: reading a loop in a flowchart
check.solution: An arrow going **back** to an earlier box is **iteration** — a loop. Because the decision controls how many times it runs, it is **indefinite** iteration, written as a WHILE.

steps.title: Tracing it
steps.body:
**Tracing is how you work out what an algorithm does, and it is examined directly.** Take one column per variable, plus the condition and any output, and a new row each time a value changes.

Never skip a row. The exam gives marks for the intermediate values, not only the final answer.

check.prompt: An algorithm sets n to 1 and doubles it while n < 50, then outputs n. What is output?
check.solution: n goes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, then **64**. At 32 the condition is still true, so it doubles once more; at 64 it fails and the loop ends. The output is **64**, not 32.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Label both exits of every decision.** A diamond with unlabelled arrows is the commonest fault in a drawn flowchart, and it costs a mark every time. Yes and No, or True and False — either is fine, but they must be there.

**Get the shape right, because the shape is the statement.** Putting `OUTPUT total` in a rectangle says it is a calculation. Putting `n ← n * 2` in a parallelogram says the user typed it. The label cannot rescue the wrong shape.

**Answer in the form the question names.** The specification says exam questions **indicate the form of response expected**. A flowchart drawn where pseudo-code was asked for is not a near miss — it does not answer the question.

**Know which way round the two pseudo-code rules go.** Pseudo-code you are **given** is always AQA's version, so reading it is not optional. Pseudo-code you **write** may be in any suitable format — the specification says so explicitly. Students often believe the opposite and waste time worrying about exact syntax.

**An algorithm must terminate.** Every flowchart needs a STOP, and every loop needs something that eventually makes its condition false. A loop whose variable never changes inside it runs forever, and spotting that in someone else's algorithm is a grade 9 observation.

**Trace with a table, not in your head.** One column per variable, plus the condition and the output, and a row for every change. The marks are in the intermediate values, and a wrong final answer with a correct trace still earns most of them.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- An **algorithm** is a sequence of steps that completes a task; a **program implements** one.
- Three representations: **pseudo-code**, **program code**, and a **flowchart**.
- **Terminal** (rounded box): START and STOP.
- **Process** (rectangle): a calculation or an assignment.
- **Input/output** (parallelogram): INPUT and OUTPUT.
- **Decision** (diamond): a question with **exactly two labelled exits**.
- Arrows show the order; an arrow **back up** is a loop.
- Every flowchart **starts and stops** with a terminal.
- AQA writes assignment with a **left arrow**: `n ← 1`.
- A decision that loops back is **indefinite iteration**, written **WHILE**.
- Pseudo-code you are **given** is always **AQA's version** — you must be able to read it.
- Pseudo-code you **write** may be in **any suitable format**.
- Questions **indicate the form of response expected**; give that form.
- **Trace with a table**: one column per variable, a row for every change.
- A loop needs something in its body that can make the condition **false**.

questions.prompt: A loop's body never changes the variable in its condition. What happens?
options: The loop never ends, because the condition can never become false
The loop runs exactly once and then carries on to the next instruction
The loop is skipped entirely and the algorithm moves past it
The program reports an error and refuses to run the algorithm
questions.solution: A WHILE loop re-tests its condition each pass. If nothing inside can change the result, the condition stays true forever and the algorithm **never terminates** — which means it is not a valid algorithm at all.

questions.prompt: Give one reason a trace table is better than working an algorithm out in your head.
questions.solution: A trace table records **every intermediate value**, so a slip is visible and the marks for the working survive even when the final answer is wrong. Held in the head, one wrong step loses everything.

questions.prompt: Describe the four flowchart symbols and what each is used for, and explain how a flowchart shows selection and iteration.
questions.solution:
A flowchart represents an algorithm as a set of boxes joined by arrows, and **the shape of each box carries its meaning**.

A **terminal** is a rounded box, and it marks where the algorithm **starts and stops**. Every flowchart has one at each end, because an algorithm that never finishes is not a valid algorithm.

A **process** is a rectangle, used for a calculation or an assignment — something the algorithm works out for itself, such as `n ← n * 2`.

An **input/output** box is a parallelogram, used when a value comes **from** the user or is shown **to** them: `INPUT age`, `OUTPUT total`. The distinction from a process matters, because putting output in a rectangle claims it is a calculation.

A **decision** is a diamond, holding a question with two possible answers, such as `n < 50?`.

**Selection** is shown by the decision symbol. The diamond has **exactly two exits**, and both must be **labelled** — normally Yes and No. Each exit leads to a different sequence of boxes, so the path the algorithm takes depends on the answer to the question. The two paths may later rejoin, or each may run to its own STOP. A diamond with only one exit is not selection at all: the question has no effect on what happens next.

**Iteration** is shown by an **arrow that goes back to an earlier box**. The algorithm reaches a decision, and one of its exits returns to a step that has already been carried out, so that step runs again. The loop ends when the decision takes the other exit. This is the only way a flowchart shows something happening more than once, so if there is no upward arrow, there is no loop.

For a loop to end, something **inside** it must be able to change the answer to the decision. A loop whose body never touches the variable in its condition runs forever.

questions.prompt: An algorithm inputs a number, doubles it while it is below 100, and outputs the result. Describe how you would represent this as a flowchart and as pseudo-code, and explain which form you would give in an exam.
questions.solution:
**As a flowchart**, the algorithm has five boxes joined by arrows.

It opens with a **terminal** — a rounded box holding START. An arrow leads to a **parallelogram** holding `INPUT n`, because the value comes from the user rather than being worked out.

Next comes a **diamond** asking `n < 100?`. This is the decision that controls the loop, and it needs **two labelled exits**. The **Yes** exit leads to a **rectangle** holding `n ← n * 2`, which is a process because the algorithm calculates it. From that rectangle an arrow goes **back up** to the diamond, and that returning arrow is what makes it a loop.

The **No** exit leads to a **parallelogram** holding `OUTPUT n`, then to a final **terminal** holding STOP.

**As pseudo-code**, the same algorithm is four lines:

```
n ← INPUT
WHILE n < 100
   n ← n * 2
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT n
```

The assignment uses a **left arrow**, which is AQA's notation. The decision-with-a-loop-back becomes a **WHILE**, because the number of repetitions is not known in advance — it depends on the number the user types. The indentation shows what is inside the loop, and `ENDWHILE` closes it.

Notice that the terminals have no equivalent in the pseudo-code. START and STOP exist to make a flowchart readable; the code simply begins at its first line and ends at its last.

**Which form to give in an exam is not a choice.** The specification says questions **indicate the form of response expected** — pseudo-code, program code, or a flowchart — so the answer is whichever the question names. Where pseudo-code **is** the accepted response, there is real freedom: the specification allows any suitable format and does not require AQA's own version. But that freedom is about **notation**, not about substituting a flowchart for code, or code for a flowchart.

examTechnique.body:
**Match the shape to the job**: rounded for START and STOP, rectangle for a calculation, parallelogram for input and output, diamond for a decision with **two labelled exits**.

Read the question for the **form of response** it names. You must be able to **read** AQA pseudo-code, but you may **write** your answer in any suitable format.
examinerErrors: A decision with one exit, or two exits left unlabelled.
Putting `OUTPUT` in a rectangle instead of a parallelogram.
Answering in a different form from the one the question named.
Believing AQA pseudo-code must be reproduced exactly when writing an answer.
Writing assignment with `=` instead of the left arrow `←`.
A loop whose body cannot change the condition, so it never ends.
Tracing in the head and losing the marks for the intermediate values.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer treats the **shape as the statement**, and never puts output in a process box. Every decision it draws has **two labelled exits**, and every flowchart **stops**. It knows the two pseudo-code rules point in opposite directions — **given** code is always AQA's version, **written** answers may be in any suitable format — and it gives the form the question actually names. When tracing, it builds a **table with a row for every change**, so the working earns marks even if the final value slips.
